_about: SIRE 2.0 lessons: one anonymised SIRE 2.0 observation a week, explained with the public OCIMF SIRE 2.0 Question Library guidance and the publications it references. Published only with reviewed=true AND publish=true; build.py --preview also renders drafts. Never include a vessel name, IMO, operator, inspector, inspecting company, port or date, and never quote the observation verbatim.

lessons.title: Enclosed space list missed the chain lockers and duct keel
lessons.summary3: An inspector observed that the ship's list of enclosed spaces left out the chain lockers and the duct keel. The responsible officer could not explain how the list had been put together or when it was last reviewed. The entry permit in use relied on that list to decide which spaces needed a permit, so two dangerous spaces could have been entered without one.
why_it_matters: The list is the starting point of every entry decision: a space that is not on it may be entered without a permit, gas test or attendant.
Chain lockers and duct keels can be oxygen-deficient or toxic (rusting steel, leaking pipes, adjacent tanks) and are named as enclosed spaces in the IMO recommendations.
A space that tested safe can turn dangerous later: cargo or inert gas leaking from adjacent tanks, rusting steel using up oxygen, or a change in the work.
SIRE 2.0 tests the person as well as the paper: officers are expected to explain how the list was built and how it is kept up to date.
inspector_looks_for: A company procedure that defines enclosed spaces and a ship-specific list of them, including spaces that use a controlled entry process instead of a permit.
Spot checks that spaces seen on deck and in the engine room are on the list and marked at their access.
Recent entry permits: a risk assessment, gas readings that fit the space and its previous content, a validity of no more than 12 hours, and all signatures.
An interview with the responsible officer and a rating about their roles in entry and on the permit.
Gas detectors in calibration and personal multi-gas detectors in use; rescue equipment in good order and drill records.
root_causes: The list was copied from a sister ship or a template and never checked against this ship.
Nobody was named to own and review the list.
New crew were not shown the list during familiarisation.
The procedure said 'identify enclosed spaces' but gave no method for doing it.
key_lessons: Build the list from a physical walk-down of this ship at delivery or takeover, and repeat it after any modification.
Name a responsible officer (normally the Chief Officer) to own the list, and review it at handover and in the annual SMS review.
Cross-check against the company master list; mark spaces not fitted on this ship as N/A instead of deleting them.
Include the list in familiarisation, so every officer can explain where it came from and how it is used.
check_on_board: Walk the ship with the list: every tank, void, cofferdam, duct keel, chain locker, trunk, pump room and CO2 room is on it.
The list matches the company master list. Spaces not fitted on this ship are marked N/A, not silently deleted.
Warning signs are at every access to a listed space.
Recent permits are complete, with readings at several levels, and are signed off.
Gas meters are in calibration with bump-test records, and alarm settings are known.
Rescue equipment is ready at the entrance, and the last drill was within 2 months with a realistic scenario.
discussion_questions: Which spaces near your workplace are enclosed? Show me on the list.
How can a space become dangerous after it was tested (cargo, rust, inerting, adjacent tanks)?
If the person inside collapses, what must the standby person do, and what must they not do?
What was our last near miss or incident involving entry, and what did we learn?

lessons.title: Portable gas instruments not tested, and the officer unsure of their limits in an inert atmosphere
lessons.summary3: One of the two portable multi-gas instruments in the cargo control room had last been checked with test gas more than two months earlier, although the check is due monthly. Asked about it, the officer could not say whether the instrument's flammable-gas sensor could be used in an inert atmosphere. Nor could the officer say which instrument on board should be used to measure hydrocarbon % volume in inerted tanks.
why_it_matters: Every enclosed space entry, tank entry, gas-freeing and inerting operation depends on the atmosphere reading.
A catalytic (% LFL) sensor gives unreliable readings in an oxygen-deficient atmosphere, so it cannot be used to measure hydrocarbons in an inerted tank.
A sensor poisoned by silicones, lead or H2S can read low without any warning.
An untested instrument, or an officer who does not know its limits, produces a reading the crew trusts but should not.
That is why inspectors combine a check of the records with questions to the officer.
inspector_looks_for: Instruments of the type and number required by the SMS and listed in the inventory, including one for O2 and HC % volume where inert gas or nitrogen padding is used.
Test-gas check records at the interval set by the manufacturer and the SMS, and calibration records in date.
Test gas cylinders in date, with the right concentration, and spare sensors and consumables.
Manuals on board in the working language.
An officer who can explain the sensor types, their limits in inert or over-pressure conditions, and what poisons them.
root_causes: The test-gas check is not in the planned maintenance system or a routine, so it slips when the officer changes or the ship is busy.
Familiarisation covers how to switch the instrument on, not what each sensor can and cannot measure.
Instruments on board are treated as interchangeable, so nobody knows which one is meant for inerted tanks.
key_lessons: No test, no entry: an instrument without a recent test-gas check is not fit to clear a space.
Know which instrument measures what: % LFL in air, % volume HC in inert atmospheres, O2, H2S and CO.
If a reading is doubtful, or the two instruments disagree, stop and use the second instrument before anyone goes in.
Record every test-gas check and do an operational check before each use.
check_on_board: Type and number of instruments match the SMS and the inventory: at least two that measure O2, LFL, H2S and CO, plus one for O2 and HC % volume in inert atmospheres where inert gas or nitrogen padding is used.
Test-gas checks done at the manufacturer and SMS interval, at least monthly and after any fault, and recorded, with an operational check before each use.
Calibration in date as the manufacturer requires (ashore or on board), with records on file; disposable personal monitors show commissioning and expiry dates and are withdrawn on expiry.
Test gas cylinders in date with the right concentration, and spare sensors, filters, tubes and other consumables on board.
Manuals on board in the working language, and officers can explain the sensor technology, the inert and over-pressure limits, and what poisons the sensors.
Officers know when personal monitors must be worn: enclosed space, tank or pumproom entry, and cargo or bunkers containing H2S.
discussion_questions: Which of our instruments can measure HC in an inerted tank, which cannot, and why?
What can poison a catalytic sensor, and how would you notice?
If the two instruments give different readings before an entry, what do you do?
toolbox_plan: Minute 1: the observation and why it matters.
Minutes 2-3: hold one of our own instruments, show its last test-gas check and calibration date, name its sensors, and say which readings are valid in an inert atmosphere.
Minute 4: do a live bump test as the manual describes, and record it.
Minute 5: rule of the day: no test, no entry; if the reading is doubtful, stop and use the second instrument.
